results.title: The determinant is affine along a rank-one direction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field, let $B$ be a square matrix over $K$ indexed by a finite type $n$, and let $u, v \in K^n$. Then for every $t \in K$, $\det(B + t\,uv^{\mathsf T}) = \det B + t\,(\det(B + uv^{\mathsf T}) - \det B)$.

results.title: First-order term of the determinant
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $A$ and $B$ be square matrices over $R$ indexed by a finite type $n$. The first-order term of the determinant of $B$ in the direction $A$ is $L_B(A) = \sum_{i \in n} \det B^{(i)}$, where $B^{(i)}$ is the matrix $B$ with its $i$-th row replaced by the $i$-th row of $A$.

results.title: The coefficient of $X$ in $\det(B + XA)$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $A$ and $B$ be square matrices over $R$ indexed by a finite type $n$. Regard $B + XA$ as a matrix over the polynomial ring $R[X]$. Then the coefficient of $X$ in the polynomial $\det(B + XA)$ equals the first-order term of the determinant $L_B(A) = \sum_{i \in n} \det B^{(i)}$, where $B^{(i)}$ is the matrix $B$ with its $i$-th row replaced by the $i$-th row of $A$.

results.title: Additivity of the first-order term of the determinant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $A$, $B$, $C$ be square matrices over $R$ indexed by a finite type $n$. Write $L_B(A) = \sum_{i \in n} \det B^{(i)}_A$, where $B^{(i)}_A$ is the matrix $B$ with its $i$-th row replaced by the $i$-th row of $A$. Then $L_B(A + C) = L_B(A) + L_B(C)$.

results.title: Homogeneity of the first-order term of the determinant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $a \in R$, and let $A$ and $B$ be square matrices over $R$ indexed by a finite type $n$. Write $L_B(A) = \sum_{i \in n} \det B^{(i)}_A$, where $B^{(i)}_A$ is the matrix $B$ with its $i$-th row replaced by the $i$-th row of $A$. Then $L_B(aA) = a \, L_B(A)$.

results.title: Essential range
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$. The essential range of $\varphi$ with respect to $\mu$ is the set of $z \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $\mu(\{x \in \alpha : |\varphi(x) - z| < \varepsilon\}) > 0$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$.

results.title: The essential range is invariant under almost-everywhere equality
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi, \psi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$. If $\varphi = \psi$ $\mu$-almost everywhere, then $\varphi$ and $\psi$ have the same essential range with respect to $\mu$.

results.title: Points outside the essential range
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$, let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ and let $z \in \mathbb{C}$. Then $z$ is not in the essential range of $\varphi$ with respect to $\mu$ if and only if there is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that the preimage under $\varphi$ of the open ball $B(z, \varepsilon) = \{w \in \mathbb{C} : |w - z| < \varepsilon\}$ has $\mu$-measure zero.

results.title: Essential range of a constant function
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ with $\mu(\alpha) \neq 0$, and let $c \in \mathbb{C}$. Then the essential range of the constant function $x \mapsto c$ with respect to $\mu$ is $\{c\}$.

results.title: Essential range for counting measure on a finite type
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite type with a measurable structure in which singletons are measurable, and let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$. Then the essential range of $\varphi$ with respect to counting measure on $\alpha$ is the range $\varphi(\alpha)$.

results.title: Constant functions are essentially bounded
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ and let $c \in \mathbb{C}$. The constant function $x \mapsto c$ belongs to $\mathcal{L}^\infty(\mu)$: it is almost everywhere strongly measurable and essentially bounded.

results.title: An essentially bounded multiple of an $L^2$ function is in $L^2$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$, let $\varphi \colon \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be an essentially bounded, almost everywhere strongly measurable function, and let $f \in L^2(\mu)$. Then the pointwise product $x \mapsto \varphi(x) f(x)$, formed with a representative of $f$, belongs to $\mathcal{L}^2(\mu)$: it is almost everywhere strongly measurable and square integrable.

results.title: Multiplication operator on $L^2$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi \colon \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be an essentially bounded, almost everywhere strongly measurable function. The multiplication operator $M_\varphi$ is the continuous $\mathbb{C}$-linear operator on $L^2(\mu)$ that sends $f$ to the class of the pointwise product $x \mapsto \varphi(x) f(x)$.

results.title: Multiplication operators with almost everywhere equal multipliers coincide
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi, \psi \colon \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be essentially bounded, almost everywhere strongly measurable functions. If $\varphi = \psi$ $\mu$-almost everywhere, then the multiplication operators $M_\varphi$ and $M_\psi$ on $L^2(\mu)$ are equal.

results.title: Measurable representatives of essentially bounded functions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be in $L^\infty(\mu)$, that is, $\mu$-almost everywhere strongly measurable and essentially bounded. results.title: Pointwise bound by the essential supremum norm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be in $L^\infty(\mu)$, that is, $\mu$-almost everywhere strongly measurable and essentially bounded. results.title: Almost everywhere bound for a multiplication operator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$, let $\varphi \colon \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be an essentially bounded, almost everywhere strongly measurable function, and let $M_\varphi$ be the multiplication operator on $L^2(\mu)$. If $C$ is a real number with $|\varphi(x)| \le C$ for $\mu$-almost every $x$, then $\|M_\varphi f\| \le C \|f\|$ for every $f \in L^2(\mu)$.

results.title: Bound for a multiplication operator on the support of a vector
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$, let $\varphi \colon \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be an essentially bounded, almost everywhere strongly measurable function, and let $M_\varphi$ be the multiplication operator on $L^2(\mu)$. If $C$ is a real number and $f \in L^2(\mu)$ is such that, for $\mu$-almost every $x$, either $|\varphi(x)| \le C$ or $f(x) = 0$, then $\|M_\varphi f\| \le C \|f\|$.

results.title: Norm bound for multiplication operators on L²
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be in $L^\infty(\mu)$, with essential supremum norm $\|\varphi\|_\infty$. Then the multiplication operator $M_\varphi$ on the complex space $L^2(\mu)$ has operator norm $\|M_\varphi\| \le \|\varphi\|_\infty$.

results.title: Normalized indicator of a set of finite positive measure
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ and let $t \subseteq \alpha$ be a measurable set with $0 < \mu(t) < \infty$. Then there is $u \in L^2(\mu)$ (complex valued) with $\|u\| = 1$ such that $u(x) = \mu(t)^{-1/2}$ for $\mu$-almost every $x \in t$ and $u(x) = 0$ for $\mu$-almost every $x \notin t$.

results.title: Norm of an L² multiplication operator with measurable multiplier
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be a measurable function in $L^\infty(\mu)$, with essential supremum norm $\|\varphi\|_\infty$. Then the multiplication operator $M_\varphi$ on the complex space $L^2(\mu)$ has operator norm $\|M_\varphi\| = \|\varphi\|_\infty$.

results.title: Norm of a multiplication operator on L²
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be in $L^\infty(\mu)$, with essential supremum norm $\|\varphi\|_\infty$. Then the multiplication operator $M_\varphi$ on the complex space $L^2(\mu)$ has operator norm $\|M_\varphi\| = \|\varphi\|_\infty$.

results.title: Spectrum of an L² multiplication operator with measurable multiplier
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be a measurable function in $L^\infty(\mu)$. Then the spectrum of the multiplication operator $M_\varphi$, as an element of the complex algebra of bounded operators on $L^2(\mu)$, equals the essential range of $\varphi$ with respect to $\mu$.

results.title: Spectrum of a multiplication operator on L²

results.title: Eigenvalues of a multiplication operator on $L^2$, measurable multiplier
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure on a measurable space $\alpha$, let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be measurable and in $L^\infty(\mu)$, and let $M_\varphi$ be the multiplication operator $f \mapsto \varphi f$ on $L^2(\mu)$. Then $z \in \mathbb{C}$ is an eigenvalue of $M_\varphi$ if and only if $\mu(\{x \in \alpha : \varphi(x) = z\}) > 0$.

results.title: Multiplication by $x$ on $L^2((1,2))$ is bounded, bijective and self-adjoint
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L^2([1,2])$ be the real Hilbert space of square-integrable real functions for Lebesgue measure on $[1,2]$, with inner product $\langle f, g\rangle = \int_1^2 f(x)g(x)\,dx$. Let $T : L^2([1,2]) \to L^2([1,2])$ be a linear map such that for every $f$, $(Tf)(x) = x f(x)$ for almost every $x \in [1,2]$. Then $T$ is continuous and bijective, and $T = T^*$, where $T^*$ is the Hilbert space adjoint of $T$.

results.title: The inverse tangent integral at $\tan x$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be a real number with $|x| \le \pi/4$, and let $P(x) = x \log|\tan x|$ for $x \ne 0$ and $P(0) = 0$. Then $\cos x \ne 0$, the series $T(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} (-1)^k \frac{\tan^{2k+1} x}{(2k+1)^2}$ (the inverse tangent integral of $\tan x$) and $F(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{\sin((4j+2)x)}{(2j+1)^2}$ are both summable, and $T(x) = P(x) + F(x)$.

results.title: Fubini numbers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Fubini number (ordered Bell number) of a natural number $n$ is $F(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} S(n,k)\, k!$, where $S(n,k)$ is the Stirling number of the second kind.

results.title: Closure of context-free languages under union
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $L$ and $M$ are context-free languages over the same alphabet, then their union $L \cup M$ is context-free.

results.title: Closure of context-free languages under concatenation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $L$ and $M$ are context-free languages over the same alphabet, then their concatenation $LM = \{uv : u \in L,\ v \in M\}$ is context-free.

results.title: Closure of context-free languages under Kleene star
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $L$ is a context-free language, then its Kleene star $L^*$ is context-free.

results.title: Powers of a context-free language are context-free
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $L$ is a context-free language, then for every natural number $n$ the power $L^n$, the concatenation of $n$ copies of $L$ (with $L^0$ the language containing only the empty word), is context-free.

results.title: Finite languages are context-free
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every finite language is context-free.

results.title: Languages of bounded word length are context-free
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Over a finite alphabet, if $n$ is a natural number and every word of a language $L$ has length at most $n$, then $L$ is context-free.

results.title: Context-free languages are closed under homomorphic images
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ and $T'$ be alphabets, $L$ a context-free language over $T$, and $\varphi$ a map sending each letter of $T$ to a word over $T'$. Then the language of all words $\varphi(a_1) \cdots \varphi(a_n)$ with $a_1 \cdots a_n \in L$ is context-free.

results.title: Intersection of a context-free language with the language of a DFA
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $L$ is a context-free language over an alphabet $T$ and $M$ is a deterministic finite automaton over $T$ with finitely many states, then the intersection of $L$ with the language accepted by $M$ is context-free.

results.title: Intersection of a context-free language with a regular language
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $L$ is a context-free language and $R$ a regular language over the same alphabet, then $L \cap R$ is context-free.

results.title: Context-free languages are closed under letter maps
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a context-free language over an alphabet $T$ and let $f \colon T \to T'$ be a map of alphabets. Then the image of $L$ under $f$, the language $\{f(a_1) \cdots f(a_n) \mid a_1 \cdots a_n \in L\}$ over $T'$, is context-free.

results.title: Letter numbering for the substitution grammar
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a context-free grammar $g$ and a letter $a$, the number of $a$ is the position (counted from $0$) of the first occurrence of $a$ in the list of terminals occurring in the productions of $g$, or the length of that list when $a$ does not occur in it.

results.title: Letter decoding for the substitution grammar
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a context-free grammar $g$ and a natural number $k$, the letter with number $k$ is the entry at position $k$ (counted from $0$) of the list of terminals occurring in the productions of $g$; there is no such letter when $k$ is at least the length of that list.

It returns a $2^k \times 2^k$ matrix together with a pair of counts: the number of scalar multiplications and the number of scalar additions and subtractions it…

results.title: Correctness of Strassen's matrix accumulator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a non-unital, non-associative ring. For every $k \ge 0$ and all $2^k \times 2^k$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $R$, the matrix returned by Strassen's accumulator on $A$, $B$, $C$ equals $C + AB$, where $AB$ is the usual matrix product, $(AB)_{ij} = \sum_t A_{it} B_{tj}$.

results.title: Entries of Strassen's matrix accumulator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a non-unital, non-associative ring. For every $k \ge 0$, all $2^k \times 2^k$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $R$ and all indices $i, j$, the $(i, j)$ entry of the matrix returned by Strassen's accumulator on $A$, $B$, $C$ is $C_{ij} + \sum_{t} A_{it} B_{tj}$, the sum running over all $2^k$ indices $t$.

results.title: Operation counts of Strassen's matrix accumulator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a type with a zero, an addition, a subtraction and a multiplication. For every $k \ge 0$ and all $2^k \times 2^k$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $R$, Strassen's accumulator on $A$, $B$, $C$ performs exactly $7^k$ scalar multiplications and exactly $(25 \cdot 7^k - 22 \cdot 4^k)/3$ scalar additions and subtractions.

results.title: Dining-philosophers state
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A state of the three dining philosophers is a triple $(s_0, s_1, s_2)$ with each $s_i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ the phase of philosopher $i$: $0$ thinking, $1$ holding the first fork, $2$ eating (holding both forks).

results.title: Phase of a philosopher
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a state $s = (s_0, s_1, s_2)$ of the three dining philosophers and a philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, the phase of philosopher $i$ in $s$ is the component $s_i$.

results.title: Updating the phase of a philosopher
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a state $s = (s_0, s_1, s_2)$ of the three dining philosophers, a philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ and a phase $p \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, setting the phase of philosopher $i$ to $p$ gives the state obtained from $s$ by replacing the component $s_i$ by $p$ and keeping the other two components.

results.title: Dining-philosophers protocol
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A protocol for three philosophers $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ sitting between forks $0, 1, 2$ consists of two maps $\mathrm{first}, \mathrm{second}$ from $\{0, 1, 2\}$ to itself, the fork philosopher $i$ picks up first and the one it picks up second, such that for every $i$ these are its two neighbouring forks $i$ and $i + 1$ (modulo $3$) in some order: either $\mathrm{first}(i) = i$ and $\mathrm{second}(i) = i + 1$, or…

results.title: Held forks
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a protocol and a state, fork $f$ is held exactly when some philosopher $i$ either has $f$ as its first fork and is in phase $1$ or $2$, or has $f$ as its second fork and is in phase $2$ (eating).

results.title: When a philosopher can move
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a protocol and a state, philosopher $i$ can move exactly when it is thinking (phase $0$) and its first fork is not held by any philosopher, or it holds its first fork (phase $1$) and its second fork is not held by any philosopher, or it is eating (phase $2$), in which case its move puts both forks down.

results.title: Move of a philosopher
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The state obtained from $s$ when philosopher $i$ moves: the phase of $i$ advances from thinking ($0$) to holding its first fork ($1$), from $1$ to eating ($2$), and from eating back to thinking; the phases of the other philosophers are unchanged. Whether the move is allowed is not checked here.

results.title: Transition system of a dining-philosophers protocol
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a protocol $P$, the labelled transition system on the states whose labels are the philosophers: there is a transition from $s$ to $t$ labelled $i$ exactly when philosopher $i$ can move in $s$ under $P$ and $t$ is the state obtained from $s$ by the move of philosopher $i$.

results.title: The eating valuation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The valuation of the atoms $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ on the states of the dining philosophers: atom $i$ holds at a state exactly when philosopher $i$ is eating there, that is, when its phase is $2$.

results.title: Initial state of the dining philosophers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The state in which all three philosophers are thinking, that is, every phase is $0$.

results.title: Naive dining-philosophers protocol
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The protocol in which every philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ picks up fork $i$ (its left fork) first and fork $i + 1$ (modulo $3$) second.

results.title: Resource-ordered dining-philosophers protocol
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The protocol in which every philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ picks up the lower-numbered of its two forks $i$ and $i + 1$ (modulo $3$) first and the higher-numbered one second: philosophers $0$ and $1$ take fork $i$ first, and philosopher $2$ takes fork $0$ first and fork $2$ second.

results.title: The deadlock formula
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The CTL formula $\neg\,\mathsf{EX}\,\top$ over the philosophers as atoms. It holds at a state exactly when the state has no successor; in the transition system of a protocol, exactly when no philosopher can move.

results.title: Neighbours-apart formula
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, the CTL formula $\neg(p_i \wedge p_{i+1})$ over the atoms $p_0, p_1, p_2$ (one per philosopher), with indices modulo $3$. Under the valuation in which $p_j$ holds when philosopher $j$ eats, it says that the neighbouring philosophers $i$ and $i + 1$ do not eat at the same time.

results.title: The naive protocol can deadlock
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Consider the transition system of the naive protocol, in which every philosopher $i$ picks up fork $i$ first and fork $i + 1$ second (indices modulo $3$), with atom $i$ read as "philosopher $i$ is eating". Its initial state, where all philosophers are thinking, satisfies the CTL formula $\mathsf{EF}$ applied to the deadlock formula: from it, a state in which no philosopher can move is reachable.

results.title: A deadlock state of the naive protocol
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In the transition system of the naive protocol, with atom $i$ read as "philosopher $i$ is eating", the state in which every philosopher holds its first fork (every phase is $1$) satisfies the deadlock formula: no philosopher can move there.

results.title: Resource ordering prevents deadlock for the dining philosophers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In the transition system of the three dining philosophers under the resource-ordered protocol, the initial state, in which everybody thinks, satisfies the CTL formula $\mathrm{AG}\,\mathrm{EX}\,\top$: every state reachable from it has a successor, that is, some philosopher can move.

results.title: Every philosopher can still eat under resource ordering
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In the transition system of the three dining philosophers under the resource-ordered protocol, with the atom $p_j$ holding when philosopher $j$ eats, the initial state, in which everybody thinks, satisfies the CTL formula $\mathrm{AG}\,\mathrm{EF}\,p_i$ for every philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$: from every state reachable from the initial state, some state in which philosopher $i$ eats is reachable.

results.title: Mutual exclusion under the naive protocol
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every philosopher $i$, in the transition system of the naive protocol, with atom $j$ read as "philosopher $j$ is eating", the initial state satisfies $\mathsf{AG}$ applied to the formula that philosophers $i$ and $i + 1$ (indices modulo $3$) do not both eat: in no state reachable from the initial state, where all philosophers are thinking, are philosophers $i$ and $i + 1$ both eating.

results.title: Neighbours never eat together under resource ordering
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In the transition system of the three dining philosophers under the resource-ordered protocol, with the atom $p_j$ holding when philosopher $j$ eats, the initial state, in which everybody thinks, satisfies the CTL formula $\mathrm{AG}\,\neg(p_i \wedge p_{i+1})$ for every philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, with indices modulo $3$: in no state reachable from the initial state do philosophers $i$ and $i + 1$ both eat.

results.title: Enabled moves under atomic acquisition
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Philosopher $i$ can move in state $s$ when it thinks and neither of its forks $i$ and $i + 1$ (modulo $3$) is held in $s$, or when it eats (it then puts both forks down); a philosopher holding only its first fork cannot move. A fork is held as in the naive protocol: philosopher $j$ holds fork $j$ when it holds its first fork or eats, and holds fork $j + 1$ when it eats.

results.title: Move of a philosopher under atomic acquisition
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In a state $s$ (the phases of the three philosophers), the move of philosopher $i$ changes only the phase of $i$: if $i$ is thinking, it starts eating, picking up both forks at once; otherwise it goes back to thinking. The phases of the other two philosophers are unchanged.

results.title: Number of seated philosophers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The number of seated philosophers in a state $s$ is the number of philosophers that hold at least one fork in $s$, that is, whose phase is either holding the first fork or eating.

results.title: Enabled moves under a butler
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Philosopher $i$ can move in state $s$ when it can move in $s$ under the naive protocol and, if it is thinking, fewer than two philosophers hold at least one fork in $s$. Under the naive protocol each philosopher $i$ picks up the left fork $i$ first and then the right fork $i + 1$ (modulo $3$), each only when no philosopher holds it, and an eating philosopher can always put both forks down.

results.title: Atomic acquisition prevents deadlock
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In the dining philosophers transition system with atomic acquisition of both forks, every state reachable from the initial state (all three philosophers thinking) has a successor: some philosopher can move.

results.title: Under atomic acquisition every philosopher can always still eat
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In the dining philosophers transition system with atomic acquisition of both forks, for each philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, from every state reachable from the initial state (all three philosophers thinking) a state in which philosopher $i$ eats is reachable, in zero or more steps.

results.title: Mutual exclusion under atomic acquisition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In the dining philosophers transition system with atomic acquisition of both forks, for each philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, in no state reachable from the initial state (all three philosophers thinking) do philosopher $i$ and its neighbour $i + 1$ (modulo $3$) both eat.

results.title: A butler prevents deadlock
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In the dining philosophers transition system of the naive protocol under a butler, every state reachable from the initial state (all three philosophers thinking) has a successor: some philosopher can move.

results.title: Under a butler every philosopher can always still eat
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In the dining philosophers transition system of the naive protocol under a butler, for each philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, from every state reachable from the initial state (all three philosophers thinking) a state in which philosopher $i$ eats is reachable, in zero or more steps.

results.title: Mutual exclusion under a butler
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In the dining philosophers transition system of the naive protocol under a butler, for each philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, in no state reachable from the initial state (all three philosophers thinking) do philosopher $i$ and its neighbour $i + 1$ (modulo $3$) both eat.
